subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage:
Friday: At Santosh's fifth birthday, Mummy puts one big bowl of toffees on the mat. Santosh grabs two fistfuls. Reena, five, sees him and grabs fast too. In a minute the bowl is empty. Two little ones get nothing.
Sunday: Nani puts out a plate of chikki. Santosh and Reena both lunge. A piece falls and breaks.
Tuesday: At the park, Reena holds out her biscuit packet. Santosh reaches for three. Reena snatches it back. "You always take all!"

qa.q: How many children got nothing at the birthday?
qa.a: Two little ones got nothing.

qa.q: Why did Reena grab fast at the birthday?
qa.a: Reena was worried that if she waited, Santosh would take everything and she would get none.

qa.q: What could Mummy try next time with the toffees?
qa.a: Mummy could give each child a small plate or let them take turns, so no one feels they must grab to get any.

qa.q: How might the two little ones feel when the bowl was empty?
qa.a: They probably felt left out and sad, watching the older children take everything first.

grounding: Over a few days, young children grab quickly from shared bowls because waiting means others will take it, leaving the group's treats drained.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: The power went out at the wedding just as the aunties set down one bowl of laddoos for the children. In the dark, Damini, five, heard hands rustling. She grabbed four laddoos and stuffed two in her frock pocket. Abhinav, six, grabbed five. "If I don't, the big kids will take them," he whispered. When the lights came back, the bowl was bare. A little girl in a pink lehenga was crying; she'd got none. Damini looked at the squashed, sticky laddoos in her pocket, then at the crying girl.

qa.q: How many laddoos did Damini grab?
qa.a: Damini grabbed four laddoos.

qa.q: What was Abhinav worried about when he grabbed five?
qa.a: Abhinav was anxious that the big kids would take all the laddoos if he waited.

qa.q: What might help children share a bowl like this more fairly?
qa.a: An adult could hand out laddoos one by one, or count them out, so the children don't feel they must rush to get any.

qa.q: How might the girl in the pink lehenga see what happened?
qa.a: She likely felt sad and left out, seeing that others had grabbed so much that none was left for her.

grounding: In a dark, crowded wedding, children grab from a shared bowl because others might take it first, and the treats quickly run out.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: At the Saturday movie night on their Pune building's terrace, Mehak's mother set one big tub of popcorn between the six children. Uday, five, took a huge handful. Mehak, six, saw him and grabbed an even bigger one, spilling half on the mat. The others copied. In minutes the tub was empty, and the movie had just started. "I want more," Uday said. Mehak's mother shook her head. "That was all of it." Mehak held her one leftover kernel and frowned. Most of it was on the mat.

qa.q: How many children shared the tub of popcorn?
qa.a: The tub was set between the six children.

qa.q: What does Mehak's frown at her one leftover kernel suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt disappointed and a bit puzzled, realising that grabbing fast had left almost nothing to eat.

qa.q: How could Mehak's mother share the popcorn next time?
qa.a: She could give each child a small bowl, so no one has to grab and less is wasted on the floor.

qa.q: What was it like for Uday when he saw the empty tub?
qa.a: Uday felt let down and still hungry, wanting more when there was none left.

grounding: Children grab from a shared popcorn tub because others will take it, and the group's treat is used up and wasted.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage:
Wednesday
Today I left the tap in the school ground running after I washed my tiffin. I thought, it's just one tap, and I was late for PT. Zeenat said she did the same yesterday. So did the boys from 5B.
After lunch there was no water at all. The whole tank was empty. Nobody could wash their hands. Ma'am said the tank fills only once a day, and today it ran out because taps were left open. The little kids from class one cried because they were thirsty.
I felt my face get hot. I didn't tell anyone it was me. But I kept thinking: if everyone thinks one tap doesn't matter, then every tap is left on.
Tomorrow I am going to close every tap I pass, even if it's not mine.
- Nirmala

qa.q: How often does the tank fill?
qa.a: The tank fills only once a day.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel when the little kids cried?
qa.a: Nirmala felt ashamed and guilty, face getting hot, knowing that open tap was part of the problem.

qa.q: What small step does Nirmala plan, and why could it help?
qa.a: Nirmala plans to close every tap on the way, which could save water and show others that each person's choice matters.

qa.q: How might the class-one children experience the empty tank?
qa.a: They were thirsty and upset, suffering from a problem they didn't cause.

grounding: A child leaves a school tap running thinking one share doesn't matter, and when everyone does the same, the shared water runs out.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: Behind the temple in their village, the pond used to be where Hemant and his sister Swati caught tadpoles. This summer Hemant, eleven, tossed his chips packet in without thinking. Everyone did. The chai-stall owner threw paper cups; the older boys dumped their bottles after cricket. One packet can't hurt, Hemant told himself. By June the pond smelled like rotten eggs. A green scum covered the water, and the buffaloes wouldn't drink from it. Swati found a dead fish floating near the steps. "Who did this?" she asked. Hemant opened his mouth, then shut it. He remembered all the packets he had thrown. So had everyone else, probably. They stood on the stone steps, looking at the ruined pond, and he felt sick in his stomach.

qa.q: What did Swati find near the steps?
qa.a: Swati found a dead fish floating near the steps.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling as he looked at the ruined pond?
qa.a: Hemant felt guilty and sick, remembering all the packets he had thrown.

qa.q: What could Hemant and Swati do next?
qa.a: They could start by picking up the rubbish they see and ask the village elders to put a bin near the pond, so everyone has another choice.

qa.q: How does Swati see the pond compared to before?
qa.a: Swati is upset and shocked, remembering it as a place for tadpoles now spoiled by rubbish.

grounding: A child litters the shared village pond thinking one packet doesn't matter, and when everyone does the same the pond is spoiled.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: At Nour's school in Amman, there was one good football for the whole of year four. Nour, nine, always grabbed it first at break and kept it until the bell, even when others were waiting. Why not? Hana did the same when she got it first, and so did the boys from the other class. Everyone kicked it hard against the wall, left it out in the rain, and nobody ever returned it to the box. One Monday the ball came back flat, a split down the side. The PE teacher held it up. "This belonged to all of you. Now it belongs to none of you." Nour stared at the ground. Break that day was long and boring. Hana kicked a stone. "It wasn't only you," she said. "It was everyone." That didn't make Nour feel any better.

qa.q: What did the PE teacher say about the ball?
qa.a: The PE teacher said, "This belonged to all of you. Now it belongs to none of you."

qa.q: How did Nour feel when the teacher held up the flat ball?
qa.a: Nour felt ashamed and guilty, staring at the ground, knowing the hogging and rough use were partly Nour's doing.

qa.q: How could year four look after a new ball?
qa.a: They could agree on turns at break, and on returning the ball to the box, so everyone plays and it lasts.

qa.q: How does Hana see the blame for the ball?
qa.a: Hana feels it was everyone's fault, not only Nour's, which shows she knows she was part of the problem too.

grounding: A child hogs and misuses a shared football thinking one share doesn't matter; when everyone does the same, the ball is ruined.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: The biology project on water testing was due Friday, and Pankaj, fifteen, had been watching his group all week in the school lab. Bhupen and Lata stayed back every day, labelling bottles, recording results. The other three, including Pankaj, kept saying, "We'll do the chart tomorrow." On Thursday, Pankaj walked in late and saw Bhupen redoing a graph someone had promised and never made. Bhupen didn't look up. His jaw was tight. "Ask your friends why they have time for cricket," he said to no one. Lata said nothing, but her eyes were red. Pankaj felt a jolt of shame. Nobody had been given a job with their name on it; so the two careful ones had quietly done everything, and now they were angry. He picked up a marker. "Tell me which part is mine," he said.

qa.q: What was Bhupen redoing when Pankaj walked in?
qa.a: Bhupen was redoing a graph someone had promised and never made.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he saw Bhupen's tight jaw?
qa.a: Pankaj felt a jolt of shame, recognising that he and the others had left the work to the two careful members.

qa.q: What could the group do to avoid this in the next project?
qa.a: They could give each person a named job with a deadline at the start, so no one can free ride and the load is shared.

qa.q: How does Bhupen feel about carrying the work?
qa.a: Bhupen feels resentful and angry, as his remark about cricket and his tight jaw show.

grounding: A student sees classmates leave group work to two diligent members and recognises that without accountability the careful ones carry the load and resent it.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage:
Dear Nazia didi,
You asked how the history project went. Honestly, I've been watching something that bothers me.
There are five of us. From the first week, Anu and Rafi did everything: the research, the model, even printing. The rest of us just added our names. Every time the class group chat had a question, Anu answered in ten minutes and the rest of us sent thumbs-up stickers.
Yesterday, at the practice presentation, Anu snapped. She said, "Do the three of you even know what our topic is?" Rafi didn't defend us. He just looked tired.
I realised no one was ever given a specific task, so it was easy to let the careful ones do it. And now they're angry, and they have a right to be. I'm going to ask Sir if we can split the next part by name.
Karthik

qa.a: Anu answered in ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Karthik seem to feel after the practice presentation?
qa.a: Karthik seems uncomfortable and guilty, recognising that the others were right to be angry.

qa.a: Clear, named tasks make everyone accountable, so the careful members don't end up carrying everything.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: Kunal, you asked why I went quiet in our group chat. Okay. I'm Abhinav, and in our chemistry project, I watched something happen and I didn't like what I saw in myself. Shreya and Farhan did everything. Every time a deadline came, they stayed up. The rest of us, me included, kept saying, "I'll do the conclusion," and never did. There was no list, no names next to tasks. So the two most careful people just picked up the slack. Last week Shreya sent a message: "Are the rest of you even part of this?" Farhan left the group chat for a day. I realised: when nobody is responsible, the responsible ones get crushed. They don't just get tired, they start resenting the whole team. So I messaged them and said I'll do the conclusion tonight, and I did.

qa.q: Which part did Abhinav finally do?
qa.a: Abhinav did the conclusion that night.

qa.q: What did Abhinav feel on seeing what was happening in the group?
qa.a: Abhinav felt uneasy and ashamed, not liking what that moment showed about Abhinav's own behaviour.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage:
Week one: Baljeet, twenty, moved into a four-person flat in Chandigarh. By Thursday there were three greasy pans in the sink. Baljeet added a plate. Someone else will do them, Baljeet thought.
Week three: The sink was full, the counter sticky. Neelam, the flatmate from Shimla, came home, sighed, and ordered takeaway instead of cooking. Baljeet did the same. One more plastic box went into the overflowing bin.
Week five: A cockroach crawled out of the stack. Everyone stood in the kitchen, arms crossed. "It's not all mine," said one. "I only left one mug," said another. Baljeet realised every one of them had believed their own bit hardly counted. Neelam said quietly, "So all of us made this." They finally cleaned together, four people and a lot of soap, till midnight.

qa.q: What crawled out of the stack in week five?
qa.a: A cockroach crawled out of the stack.

qa.q: What was Baljeet thinking when adding a plate in week one?
qa.a: Baljeet felt calm and unbothered, assuming someone else would do the dishes, a careless thought.

qa.q: What could the flatmates agree to so this doesn't happen again?
qa.a: They could set a simple dish rota or rule to wash one's own plates the same day, so no one's small share piles up.

qa.q: How might Neelam see the kitchen on coming home in week three?
qa.a: Neelam felt tired and discouraged, choosing takeaway rather than face the mess everyone had left.

grounding: Flatmates each leave a little mess in a shared kitchen, assuming someone else will clean, until the mess grows and everyone suffers.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: Sarika, you're complaining about your flat's kitchen? Let me tell you about the Room 12 kitchen in our boys' hostel at the engineering college, 1996. I'm Saurabh, and there were eight of us sharing one small stove. Everyone cooked instant noodles at midnight and left the pan. I did too. I thought: one pan, what's one pan? By the end of term, the pans had grown fungus. Somebody's milk had turned to cheese in a cupboard. Rats moved in. We stopped cooking and spent all our pocket money on the canteen. Every single one of us blamed the others. Nobody thought it was his own pan that had started it. Finally the warden locked the kitchen for a month. Only then did we sit together, eight fools, and agree who cleaned which day.

qa.q: How many students shared the Room 12 kitchen?

qa.q: What was Saurabh thinking when leaving his pan?
qa.a: Saurabh thought one pan didn't matter, feeling careless and sure his share was too small to count.

qa.q: How might the warden have felt about locking the kitchen?
qa.a: The warden was probably fed up and frustrated, seeing that the students would not fix the mess themselves.

grounding: An elder recalls a hostel kitchen where each person left a little mess, assuming others would clean, until everyone suffered.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
passage: The PG's water tank had run dry again, and there were only two buckets for the whole floor until evening. Sudha, twenty-one, looked into the shared kitchen: every vessel was dirty, a pot of dal was growing a skin, and someone's tea strainer had turned black. She had added her own plate on Monday; she'd been sure someone would wash up. So, it seemed, had Dhruv and the three others. Now there wasn't even water to cook rice. Dhruv came in, saw the mess, and groaned. "Who left all this?" Sudha opened her mouth to say "not me," then stopped. Her plate was on top. So was his mug. "All of us," she said. With the little water they had, they washed just enough to cook one meal together. The rest had to wait for the tanker.

qa.q: How many buckets were there for the whole floor?
qa.a: There were only two buckets for the whole floor.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she stopped herself from saying "not me"?
qa.a: Sudha felt uncomfortable and guilty, seeing her own plate on top of the pile.

qa.q: What could the PG's residents do once the water returns?
qa.a: They could agree a daily washing rota or each wash their own vessels at once, so no one assumes someone else will.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel when Sudha said "All of us"?
qa.a: Dhruv might feel caught out and a little embarrassed, recognising that his mug was part of it too.

grounding: Flatmates each leave a little mess in a shared kitchen, assuming someone else will clean, until everyone suffers, made worse by a water shortage.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
subtype: Setting rules everyone can live with [Response]
passage: Tushar, you asked on the call how our lane fixed the water pump fights. Okay, here's what happened. I'm Nitin, twenty-five, and in our Nagpur lane twelve houses share one hand pump. People used to fill ten buckets while others waited, then fight. So at the residents' meeting I proposed three things. One, a rota board with each house's time slot. Two, a limit of four buckets per turn. Three, one person from each side of the lane checks the board each week, taking turns. People grumbled. So I went first. For a whole month I only filled my four buckets, even when my slot came and nobody was waiting. My neighbours saw that. When Sharma-uncle filled six, the checker just pointed at the board, and he laughed and poured two back. No shouting. It's not perfect, but the fights stopped.

qa.q: How many houses share the hand pump?
qa.a: Twelve houses share one hand pump.

qa.q: What does Nitin's month of filling only four buckets suggest about Nitin's thinking?
qa.a: It suggests Nitin felt determined to earn trust, knowing people would only follow a rule they saw Nitin keep.

qa.q: Why did the rota work better than the old system?
qa.a: It gave clear slots and limits, shared checking and a leader who modelled it, so fairness was visible and people trusted it.

qa.q: How might Sharma-uncle have felt when the checker pointed at the board?
qa.a: Sharma-uncle seemed a little embarrassed but good-humoured, laughing and pouring two buckets back because the rule was clearly fair.

grounding: A young adult proposes a fair rota, clear limits and shared monitoring for a common pump, models it first, and the lane protects its water through trust.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
subtype: Setting rules everyone can live with [Response]
passage: I live on the second floor of the same Bengaluru building as Gautam, so I saw the washing-machine business from start to finish. The one shared machine in the basement was always full of someone's forgotten clothes. People dumped wet laundry on the floor, and last month it broke from overloading. Gautam, maybe twenty-four, came to the residents' chat group with a plan: a sign-up sheet on the door, one load per flat per slot, and a rota for checking the filter every Sunday, starting with him. He also suggested a small fine into a repair jar if someone overloaded it. Some people argued. But I saw him, for two weeks, empty his load exactly on time and clean the filter himself. By the third week, others were writing their names. I don't know if he was nervous about it. He looked calm. The machine hasn't broken since.

qa.q: What was put on the door of the basement?
qa.a: A sign-up sheet was put on the door.

qa.q: What does Gautam's calm manner suggest about how he felt proposing the rules?
qa.a: It suggests Gautam felt steady and confident, though the narrator admits not knowing whether he was nervous inside.

qa.q: Which part of Gautam's approach helped most, and why?
qa.a: Following the rules himself for two weeks made the system look fair and trustworthy, so others joined willingly.

qa.q: How might residents who argued at first see the new system later?
qa.a: They may have come round once they saw it working fairly and the machine stopped breaking.

grounding: A neighbour watches a young adult propose a sign-up rota, limits and shared checks for a common washing machine, model them first, and win trust.

subtopic: Tragedy of the commons
subtype: Setting rules everyone can live with [Response]
passage:
Week one: In their Hyderabad office, the shared fridge smelled terrible. Chaitanya, twenty-six, opened it to find three-week-old biryani and five unlabelled boxes. Mohit from accounts shrugged. "Everyone does it."

Week five: Mohit, on his Friday, found a box with no label and quietly binned it. Someone grumbled. Mohit pointed at the rota. "Rule's for everyone. Chaitanya binned his own curd." The fridge now smells like nothing at all.

qa.a: Clear labels, a weekly rota and Chaitanya modelling it first, even with his own food, made fairness visible and built trust.

qa.q: How did Mohit's view change from week one to week five?
qa.a: Mohit moved from shrugging that everyone does it to enforcing the rule himself, showing he now trusted the system.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
subtype: Share or cheat in a game [Actor]
passage: During recess at the school's board-game club, Vishal, ten, and Akash were playing a trading game with paper cards. The rules said you each put a card face-down and swapped at the same time. If both gave good cards, you both scored. If one gave a junk card, that person got a bigger score. Vishal held his best card and looked at Akash. What if Akash gives junk? he thought. Then I'll look stupid. His hands were clammy. He slipped his best card back and put down a junk one. Akash turned his card over: the golden elephant, his best. Akash's face fell. "I trusted you," he said. Vishal had the bigger score. But he didn't feel like he'd won. He felt like the worst person in the room.

qa.q: What card did Akash put down?
qa.a: Akash put down the golden elephant, his best.

qa.q: Why did Vishal put down a junk card?
qa.a: Vishal was afraid Akash would cheat first and he'd look stupid, so fear of being the sucker drove him to cheat.

qa.q: What could Vishal try in the next round?
qa.a: Vishal could apologise and play his good card, showing Akash he's willing to cooperate even if it feels risky.

qa.q: How did Akash experience Vishal's choice?
qa.a: Akash felt hurt and betrayed, his face falling as he said "I trusted you."

grounding: A child in a trading game fears his friend will cheat first and so cheats himself, winning points but feeling bad.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection

passage: Farida, you think your friend will trick you in the card game, so you'll trick him first? Let me tell you about me and Bablu. I'm Arnab dadu, and when I was ten in Kolkata we traded marbles. The rule was: we'd each put our marbles in a cloth bag and swap bags at the same time. Fair trade, everybody happy. But one day I thought, what if Bablu puts pebbles instead of marbles? I'd look like a fool before the whole para. So I filled my bag with pebbles. Bablu's bag had his best glass marbles, the blue ones. When he saw the pebbles, he just walked away. subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: Dolma and Noor, both fifteen, had a joint presentation on the city's lakes due Monday at their Bengaluru school. They'd split it: Dolma would research, Noor would make the slides. But Dolma thought, Noor's good with slides; she'll fill in whatever's missing. And Noor thought, Dolma always over-prepares; she'll cover for me. So Dolma spent Saturday at a cousin's wedding, and Noor spent Sunday on a video marathon. On Monday morning, they met at the gate. Dolma had two pages of notes. Noor had four slides with no text. They looked at each other and understood. In front of the class, they stumbled and repeated each other. They got a C. If both had done their parts, they would have got an A. On the bus home, neither spoke.

qa.q: What grade did Dolma and Noor get?
qa.a: They got a C.

qa.q: What was Dolma thinking when she chose to go to the wedding?
qa.a: Dolma felt relaxed and sure Noor would fill in whatever was missing, so it seemed safe to shirk.

qa.q: What could the girls have done differently?
qa.a: They could have checked in with each other on Saturday and set deadlines for each part, so neither could quietly rely on the other.

qa.q: How might Noor feel on the silent bus ride home?
qa.a: Noor probably felt embarrassed and guilty, knowing her shortcut hurt both of them.

grounding: Two teenagers preparing a joint presentation each shirk, expecting the other to cover, and both end up worse than if they had cooperated.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage:
"Did you finish your half?" Irfan asked, catching Mohit at the canteen.
"Almost. You?"
"Almost." Irfan paused. "Honestly, I thought you'd do the conclusion. You're better at it."
"What? I thought you'd do it. You always write more."
"So... who did the graphs?"
"You said you'd do the graphs."
"I said I'd look at them."
They both stared at the laptop. The presentation was in two hours.
"This is bad," Mohit said.
"We both just waited for the other one."
"Yeah." Mohit rubbed his face. "If we'd split it properly, we'd be done."
"Okay. You do graphs, I'll do the conclusion. Now."
They worked in silence. In class they got through it, just. The teacher wrote: "Uneven. Seems rushed." Mohit crumpled the paper. "Next time we write down who does what."
